question: Eating carrots improves your night vision.

evidence.title: Vitamin A and Carotenoids: Fact Sheet for Consumers
evidence.excerpt: One of the first signs of vitamin A deficiency is night blindness, the inability to see in low light or darkness. Beta-carotene from foods such as carrots is converted into vitamin A.

evidence.title: A WWII Propaganda Campaign Popularized the Myth That Carrots Help You See in the Dark
evidence.excerpt: The British Air Ministry spread the story that its pilots ate carrots to explain their success at night, hiding the use of new airborne radar.

evidence.title: Do carrots really improve your eyesight?
evidence.excerpt: If you already get enough vitamin A, eating more carrots will not sharpen your night vision. Extra beta-carotene simply isn't converted.

evidence.title: Dark adaptation improves with vitamin A from foods in night-blind pregnant women
evidence.excerpt: Among night-blind pregnant women in Nepal, daily carrots restored dark adaptation as well as vitamin A capsules over six weeks.

turns.text: ev1 and ev4 support a benefit, but only for people who lack vitamin A. ev2 and ev3 refute the general claim for well-fed people. The claim overgeneralises.
ev1 and ev4 show carrots restore night vision. ev2 is about the origin of the story and ev3 adds a caveat; neither shows carrots don't help.
Two sources show a direct effect on night vision (ev1, ev4). ev2 says the wartime story was exaggerated. ev3 limits the effect to deficient diets.

rationale: Stance count: two sources support the claim with all three graders agreeing; the refuting reads of ev2 and ev3 were split. Aggregated stance leans supported, with low confidence.
reasons: Vitamin A from carrots reverses night blindness (ev1, ev4)
